title: Command Age Timeouts and Braking Strength in Simulated Vehicle Following
abstract: A remote command can become too old to guide a moving vehicle. A backup may help, but its effect depends on brake strength, fault timing, and its action after a timeout. This study compares age limits and control architectures in a two vehicle model, without claiming to isolate early action or fresh measurements. Shared cases cover a braking leader and a leader that keeps its speed. Tests impose low delay, jitter, loss, and fixed or random outage starts. The data contain 107,200 runs based on four hundred physical cases. Collision counts and cruise distance costs are shown across the threshold sweep. Nearby limits reveal a switching boundary rather than a smooth response in the jitter profile. At the primary age limit, Remote 7 has fewer braking collisions and less cruise distance loss than Stop 7 in the loss and random outage profiles. Stop 7 avoids more collisions only under the deliberately hazard aligned fixed outage, at a cruise distance loss of about thirty five percent. This is strong nominal control versus weak nominal control with strong backup; their combination was not tested. Stratifying random outages by overlap with the full lead braking interval places most of the equal force Stop 3 benefit in the overlap group. Strong Stop 7 also helps outside that group. Full case contact scores and collision free intervention metrics complement event counts. Clock checks remain illustrative. These conditional comparisons describe the model and sampled faults, not an optimal timeout, a safety guarantee, or isolated causal effects.
